claims.text: Increasing local chemical short-range order reduces random-potential electron scattering in high-entropy superconducting alloys.
Increasing local chemical short-range order increases effective electron-phonon coupling.
The increase in effective electron-phonon coupling caused by short-range order raises the superconducting transition temperature.
A single-phase CoCrFeNiMn or similar HEA can serve as a highly chemically disordered superconducting initial state.
Annealing promotes partial chemical short-range order.
Suitable annealing can increase short-range order without inducing secondary phases or macroscopic phase separation.
Chemical short-range order changes the local atomic arrangement.
Chemical short-range order may increase the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Random-alloy electron scattering limits Cooper-pair formation.
Reduced random-alloy scattering permits stronger electron-phonon coupling in localized regions.
A fully disordered state suppresses Cooper pairing more strongly than a short-range-ordered state.
An annealed sample with greater short-range order will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than a rapidly quenched, chemically random baseline.
An annealed sample with greater short-range order may have a narrower superconducting transition than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Annealing and increased short-range order will leave the overall carrier concentration approximately unchanged.
Rapid quenching preserves a high degree of chemical randomness.
The proposed relationship is limited to alloys whose superconductivity is governed primarily by conventional electron-phonon interactions.
Secondary-phase formation or grain coarsening can prevent isolation of the proposed short-range-order effect.
The proposed relationship may not hold when magnetic fluctuations or unconventional pairing mechanisms dominate.
Residual resistivity can be used as an indicator of electron-scattering strength.
